text:
The first time I saw my father in a bathing suit, he stood at the edge of the ship’s pool with a plastic cup of orange juice, looking as if someone had asked him to explain the ocean.

His suit was blue, with tiny white anchors. His legs were thin, the skin at his knees loose. A white scar showed where his chest had been opened. After chemotherapy, his hair had grown back as soft gray fuzz, making him look, to my embarrassment, like a very old baby. He was fifty-one, though lately he seemed older. The cup trembled in his hand.

“Is this a gay thing?” I asked.

He glanced at me. “The pool?”

“The suit.”

“Fashion is for everyone.”

I was thirteen and full of questions that were really accusations. I had packed three books, black jeans, and the feeling that my father had made me an accessory to his life. His friends had organized a weeklong Caribbean cruise for gay men and said I should come along. My mother had said, “It’s your decision,” in a tone suggesting my answer would become evidence against him. My father said it would be nice to have me there.

I didn’t know what to do with “nice.” It seemed too small for the work of going.

The ship was called the Celestine, a name that suggested a hotel built by someone’s optimistic aunt. It left Miami in March with more than a thousand passengers, among them several hundred gay men, a handful of women, and me. My father had called it “a trip with friends.” When I asked about the bracelets that said OUT AT SEA, he explained. He hadn’t lied; he had simply given the truth the smallest possible berth.

At home, his being gay existed in a collection of objects and habits: a photograph of him and Peter on a Provincetown beach, dinner parties where everyone knew a joke I didn’t understand, a man sometimes leaving in the morning with my father’s shirt tucked into his trousers. I knew my father loved me. I also knew his life had rooms I couldn’t enter, which seemed a special kind of rejection.

My parents separated when I was six. My father came out when I was nine. My mother never said one thing caused the other. I assembled my own story from the silences: my father had gone away from the family, then toward something else. His friends were kind to me, but I thought of their kindness as the attention adults gave a child who belonged to someone else.

The cruise was the first time I had been asked to enter that world for more than an afternoon. I worried about being looked at, and about looking at people. I worried the men would want to talk to me about my father. I worried they wouldn’t.

At dinner the first night, I sat between my father and Reggie, a man with gold rings in both ears and a laugh that made the water glasses tremble. He asked if I liked school.

“I don’t know,” I said.

“Good answer,” he said. “Keep it.”

I stared at the menu, where every dish seemed to have been named by someone who had mistaken adjectives for food. Reggie asked what I liked to read. When I said mysteries, he recommended a detective series and spent ten minutes describing the first book without giving away the ending. He wasn’t performing for me. He was simply telling a story.

The men at the table didn’t talk about being gay. They talked about mortgages, their knees, the price of tomatoes, and whether a person could learn to like olives after forty. My father sat with his shoulders down. I hadn’t realized how often he kept them raised.

By the second day, I understood there were different ways to be the only child in a room. On the Celestine, I was the only teenager among men who didn’t regard me as a problem to solve. They spoke to me without making a spectacle of including me. If I got up, no one asked where I was going in the voice of a person checking a gate.

My father had made a list of things he wanted to do: swim, dance, visit the ship’s library, take me to San Juan, sit in the sun. He crossed off “swim” after the water made him cold and “sit in the sun” when it made him tired. He kept the list folded in his pocket.

The cancer was in his pancreas and liver. It had been found in August, and the doctors used the word terminal as if it were a weather condition. My father disliked it. He said it made an ordinary person sound like a train station. The cruise had been planned before he got sick, and he insisted on going.

“You could have gone without me,” I said in the cabin.

“I could have gone without you,” he said. “That’s not the same as wanting to.”

He sat at the desk, sorting pills into a plastic organizer. I had brought paperback books and a red cardigan because my mother said ships were cold.

“Do you think I’m making this about me?” I asked.

He stopped. “I think you’re allowed to make it about you.”

That was one of the things I didn’t like about him: he made room for my feelings before I’d decided whether I wanted to have them.

In St. Thomas, I went with him and three friends to a beach where the sand was white and the water came in so gently it seemed placed there by hand. I sat under a tree with Reggie, who had bought a coconut and was trying to keep the straw upright.

My father went into the water with Peter, holding his wrist as they stepped down the sandy slope. At one point, he turned and waved. I waved back, as I might have at the far end of a supermarket aisle.

For years, I had thought of his friends as people who had taken him away from me. Watching them help him through the water, I began to see that they had also helped him stay. They knew when he was tired, which foods he could eat, and how to let him refuse help without letting him fall. They had been building a life around him while I resented its shape.

On the fourth day I met Julian. He was fifteen, with brown hair and a small scar on his chin. He was traveling with his two fathers and his aunt, a nurse who seemed to know the location of every elevator on the ship. He sat on the floor outside the teen lounge, closed because there weren’t enough teenagers to keep it open. I was passing with a book.

“Are you also the whole youth program?” he asked.

“I’m the entire youth division.”

“I’m the deputy director.”

We sat on the floor and talked. He was bored with the book he’d brought, about a boy who built a boat. One of his dads was obsessed with bird-watching; the other pretended not to be. I told him my father had a list of things he wanted to do and was crossing them off at random. We discussed whether cruise ships were ships or hotels that had moved somewhere inconvenient.

It was my first real conversation with a boy, if “real” means I didn’t spend the whole time imagining how I seemed from the outside. I didn’t have to be pretty or clever or indifferent. I didn’t have to explain what my father was. Julian already understood that having two fathers was the least interesting fact about a person. He asked if my father was sick. I said yes. He said he was sorry. Then we talked about the sharks on his shirt.

The next day, we sat with our feet in the pool. Julian told me that people sometimes asked which of his fathers was the real one.

“What do you say?” I asked.

“Depends how annoying they are.”

I laughed. “What if they’re not annoying?”

“Then I say both.”

The answer was so simple I felt I should have known it. Around us, men in sunglasses read, slept, and rubbed sunscreen onto each other’s shoulders. Nobody seemed to be studying Julian and me or my father. I had spent years thinking his life was visible in a way that made it fragile. On the ship, it looked sturdy: it had routines, old arguments, bad jokes, and people who knew which side hurt when he reached for a glass.

That afternoon, my father and I went to the ship’s library, a room with six books and a large window. He chose a book of poems and asked if I liked poetry.

“Some of the words,” I said.

“That’s a start.”

He read me a poem about a man looking at the sea. He stopped twice to catch his breath. Each time, I pretended to look out the window. I didn’t want him to feel watched. I also didn’t want him to feel alone. I hadn’t yet worked out that those wishes could conflict.

That evening there was a dance in the ballroom. My father had been looking forward to it. He wore a white shirt and blue jacket; I wore the red cardigan over a dress I’d brought because my mother said there might be a formal night.

“You look like you’re going to a school dance,” he said, looking at me in the mirror.

“I am.”

“I’m honored.”

“Don’t be weird.”

“I’ll try.”

The ballroom was full of men. The band played a song I knew from the radio, and couples danced with a confidence that made me shy and curious. My father came over and offered his hand.

“You don’t have to,” he said.

I went with him.

He was light in my arms. I felt the hard ridge of his shoulder through his jacket. My mother used to say he could dance his way out of an argument. I remembered him dancing with her at a wedding when I was small, his hand on her back, both of them smiling as if the night would go on forever.

Now he counted under his breath. “One, two, three. Don’t think so much.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re thinking about how much you’re not thinking.”

“Dad.”

“Sorry.”

The song ended. He held my hand for a moment, then let go. Back at the table, Julian stood at the edge of the dance floor with one of his fathers. He raised his eyebrows as if to ask whether I’d survived. I nodded.

The rest of the week passed in scenes: my father eating two bites of mango and giving me the rest; Reggie singing a show tune to the moon from our balcony; Julian and me leaning over the rail to watch flying fish skim the water; Peter tucking a blanket around my father’s legs when he fell asleep in a deck chair. The ship kept moving. My father kept getting tired.

On the last day, there was no land in sight, only blue water and an enormous sky. My father slept through lunch and woke in the late afternoon. He asked me to help him dress for dinner. I found his blue jacket and fastened the top button because his fingers were shaking.

“Thank you,” he said.

At dinner, he ate almost nothing. Reggie talked about a restaurant in Chicago. Peter told a story about a cousin trying to smuggle a potted plant through airport security. My father listened, smiling. Everyone knew what was happening, and nobody needed to announce it.

Afterward, the band began to play. My father looked at me.

“One more?”

“You’re sure?”

“I’m not sure about many things.”

I took his hand.

It was the last dance my father and I had, though it didn’t feel like a last dance then. It felt like a dance after dinner, on a ship, with a band playing a song I would later hear in grocery stores and hotel lobbies and never again mistake for background music. The ballroom smelled of floor polish and cologne. My father’s hand was warm and damp. I put my cheek against his jacket and listened to his breathing, not quite a rhythm, but something that kept going.

“You’ve been very good company,” he said.

“I know.”

He laughed, and I felt it against me.

A month later, he was in the hospital. He died on a Wednesday morning in April. Peter called my mother, and my mother called me. The adults around me said the necessary things in careful voices. I was fourteen. I knew what had happened, but not what it meant to happen to me.

At the funeral, Reggie stood near the back. Julian wasn’t there, but he sent a card with a shark on the front. Inside, he wrote that I could call him if I ever wanted to talk about books, ships, or fathers. I kept the card in a drawer for years.

For a while, I thought the cruise had been a place where my father went to be happy before he died. Later I understood it was also a place where I had been happy with him. The distinction mattered. I had believed that to fit into his life, I needed to understand every part of it, approve of it, or stop feeling left out. On the ship, I learned that fitting in could mean sitting beside him while he slept, taking the fruit he couldn’t finish, letting his friends tell me stories about him. It could mean dancing without asking whether the dance belonged to me.

I’ve never been back to the Caribbean. I still remember the pool, the white plastic chairs, the orange juice trembling in my father’s hand. I remember the men in bathing suits, their shoulders bright with sun, talking about olives and mortgages and the sea. I remember Julian asking if I was the whole youth program. I remember my father’s jacket beneath my cheek, his laughter caught in the music.

When I think of him now, I don’t see a man divided between the family he left and the life he chose. I see him in the ballroom, moving carefully, counting under his breath. I see the people around him making a circle large enough for him to stay in. And I see myself there too, no longer waiting to be asked what I thought of it all, but holding his hand, learning the steps.
